verses.text: The words of Nehemiah the son of Hacaliah. Now in the month Chislev, in the twentieth year, as I was in Shushan the palace,
Hanani, one of my brothers, came, he and certain men out of Judah; and I asked them about the Jews who had escaped, who were left of the captivity, and concerning Jerusalem.
They said to me, “The remnant who are left of the captivity there in the province are in great affliction and reproach. The wall of Jerusalem is also broken down, and its gates are burned with fire.”
When I heard these words, I sat down and wept, and mourned several days; and I fasted and prayed before the God  of heaven,
and said, “I beg you, Yahweh,  the God of heaven, the great and awesome God, who keeps covenant and loving kindness with those who love him and keep his commandments:

Let your ear now be attentive, and your eyes open, that you may listen to the prayer of your servant, which I pray before you at this time, day and night, for the children of Israel your servants, while I confess the sins of the children of Israel, which we have sinned against you. Yes, I and my father’s house have sinned.
We have dealt very corruptly against you, and have not kept the commandments, nor the statutes, nor the ordinances, which you commanded your servant Moses.
“Remember, I beg you, the word that you commanded your servant Moses, saying, ‘If you trespass, I will scatter you among the peoples;

but if you return to me, and keep my commandments and do them, though your outcasts were in the uttermost part of the heavens, yet I will gather them from there, and will bring them to the place that I have chosen, to cause my name to dwell there.’
“Now these are your servants and your people, whom you have redeemed by your great power, and by your strong hand.

Lord,  I beg you, let your ear be attentive now to the prayer of your servant, and to the prayer of your servants, who delight to fear your name; and please prosper your servant today, and grant him mercy in the sight of this man.” Now I was cup bearer to the king.

footnotes.content: Nehemiah the son of Hacaliah—a name we'd forget except that God remembers the faithful. In Shushan, the very center of power, he's serving as cupbearer to a foreign king, yet his heart remains anchored to Jerusalem. Sometimes the Lord places His servants far from home so He can work through them near the throne.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: His brother Hanani arrives from Judah with news, and Nehemiah doesn't hesitate to ask: How are our people? What of Jerusalem? A man this far from home could ignore such questions, but love won't let him. He's been waiting for word; now the waiting ends.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The remnant in Jerusalem—those who returned from captivity—live in great affliction. The walls are broken; the gates burned. When Hanani speaks these words, Nehemiah hears not just facts but a wound. Every broken stone is a place where the enemy could enter, where the Lord's people lie exposed to shame.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He sits down and weeps. Not a quick tear, but days of mourning, fasting, prayer—a man undone by what he's heard. Watch how sorrow moves him: not to blame, not to despair, but to his knees. Sometimes the deepest love shows itself in tears that lead us to God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "I beg you, Yahweh, the great and awesome God." He doesn't begin with his problem; he begins with the God who keeps covenant. Before he asks for help, he reminds himself—and us—that God remembers His promises to those who love and obey Him. When our own strength fails, we lean on His faithfulness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Let your ear be attentive, let your eyes open." He's praying in the presence of a king's court, yet he speaks as if only the God of heaven can hear him. And he doesn't pray for Jerusalem only—he confesses sin, his own and his people's, knowing that repentance must come first, healing second.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "We have dealt very corruptly." No finger-pointing here. He owns the failure of the whole people, even though he himself never worshiped idols in Shushan. This is the prayer of someone who understands solidarity—we fall together, and we must repent together.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Remember the word that you commanded your servant Moses." Nehemiah quotes the covenant—if we trespass, He'll scatter us. He's not claiming innocence; he's reminding God of His own word, the ground on which he dares to pray. It's a bold move, but it rests entirely on God's promise.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "But if you return to me and keep my commandments, even from the uttermost parts of the heavens I will gather them." Here's the mercy behind the law: exile isn't final. Return is always possible. No distance is too far for God to reach and restore those who turn their hearts to Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "These are your servants and your people, whom you have redeemed by your great power." He reminds God that Jerusalem's people belong to God, not to the enemies around them. He's not asking God to do something new—only to remember what He's already done, and do it again.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo: a man of prayer serving in a foreign court, unknown to kings and courts around him, yet his name lives because he prayed for his people and God answered. The small faithful voice crying out to God in the night—that's the thread that holds history.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
